newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-BEBETO TO JOIN SPAIN'S SEVILLA.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-BEBETO TO JOIN SPAIN'S SEVILLA.

text.p: Flamengo president Kleber Leite confirmed on Wednesday that Brazil international striker Bebeto had been sold to Spanish club Sevilla after a stay of less than five months with the Rio de Janeiro club.
"The deal has been concluded," Leite said, adding that Bebeto would not play in a Brazilian championship match at home to Sport Recife later on Wednesday.
The deal is the latest of a bizarre series of comings and goings at the Rio de Janeiro club, which claims to be the best supported in Brazil.

Bebeto, 32, arrived in June when it was imagined he would team up with Romario, who partnered him in Brazil's attack in the 1994 World Cup. The two scored eight goals between them and Brazil won the trophy.
But shortly after Bebeto's arrival Romario was sold to Spanish club Valencia, only to return, on loan, 78 days later after twice falling out with coach Luis Aragones.
Within 10 days, however, Bebeto himself was on his way once again. Bebeto said that Flamengo had initiated negotiations without his knowledge.
The pair played together for less than one half in a Brazilian championship match against Internacional last month before Romario hobbled off injured. He is still not fit to return.
Instead of the dreamed Romario-Bebeto partnership, Flamengo were due to face Sport with two little-known strikers from the reserve team.
Bebeto scored seven goals in the Brazilian championship in 14 games for Flamengo but has not had a happy time.
The team are almost certain to miss a place in the play-off stage of the competition after a poor series of results which has seen them slump to 16th in the table.

Bebeto has often fought a lone battle in attack, a solitary world-class player in an otherwise mediocre team. In one game, when he failed to score, Flamengo fans jeered him and chanted the name of Romario.
Leite, whose two-year reign has seen at least 40 transfer deals, has been roundly criticised for his seemingly incoherent wheeling and dealing.
"Flamengo don't buy and sell players because they are good or bad, they buy and sell them for the sake of it," newspaper columnist Fernando Calazans said.
